title: Search Tree Common Ancestor
statement:
Find the lowest common ancestor of two values in a binary search tree.

Contract
- `root` is a non-null binary search tree with distinct values; both `p` and `q` are values that occur in it.
- The lowest common ancestor is the deepest node that has both values in its subtree. A node counts as an ancestor of itself, so the answer may be the node holding `p` or `q`. `p` and `q` may be equal and may be given in either order.
- Return the node itself (not a copy) using `Solution.TreeNode` (fields `value`, `left`, `right`). Do not modify the tree.

Examples
- In `[20, 10, 30, 5, 15, 25, 35]`, the ancestor of `5` and `15` is the node `10`.
- In the same tree, the ancestor of `5` and `35` is the root `20`.
- In the same tree, the ancestor of `10` and `15` is the node `10`, an ancestor of itself.
hints: Both values are in the tree, so ordering rules tell you which side each one lives on without searching both subtrees.
From the root: if both values are smaller than the current node, move left; if both are larger, move right.

The first node where the values split (or equal one of them) is the answer; no recursion or extra storage is needed. Intended complexity: O(h) time for tree height h (O(log n) in a balanced tree with n nodes) and O(1) extra space.
inputSyntax: Input: the tree in level order followed by the two values, for example: [20, 10, 30, 5, 15, 25, 35] 5 15
